purpose: Turn probability into surprisal, weight each information value, and see how uncertainty changes with the same return-count distribution.
meaning: The Shannon entropy of a finite random variable is its expected self-information. With logarithms to base two, the result is measured in bits. Certainty gives zero; equal masses maximize entropy among distributions on a fixed finite set of outcome values.

definition.setting: An assumed library return-desk model for X, the number of books at one future check-in: X has listed values 0,1,2.

signature.X: Random number of books at the next check-in.
signature.xᵢ: One of the three outcome values 0, 1 or 2 books.
signature.pᵢ: Probability P(X=xᵢ) assigned to outcome xᵢ.
signature.r: Share of the probability left after one-book outcomes, assigned to two books.
signature.I(xᵢ): Self-information, or surprisal, of a positive-probability outcome.
signature.H(X): Expected self-information of the whole distribution.
signature.−pᵢlog₂pᵢ: One outcome’s entropy contribution in bits.

conditions: The random variable X counts books received at the next library check-in and takes values 0, 1 or 2. These probabilities form an assumed teaching model, not collected library data.
The controls q and r lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. q is the probability of one book; r assigns a share of the remaining probability to two books. The rest goes to zero books.
The probability mass function is p₀=(1−q)(1−r), p₁=q and p₂=(1−q)r. Each mass is nonnegative and their sum is one. A zero mass removes that outcome from the support.
Logarithms use base two, so self-information and entropy have units of bits. A change of logarithm base rescales the numerical value.
For pᵢ=0 the entropy contribution is defined as zero by continuity; its self-information is not evaluated as an ordinary finite numerical value.
For three listed outcome values, 0≤H(X)≤log₂3. The upper bound is reached when all three masses are 1/3; a single unit mass gives zero entropy.
definition.domain_notes: This lesson uses finite Shannon entropy of a discrete distribution. It does not implement continuous differential entropy, physical entropy, conditional entropy or a coding algorithm.
definition.proof_status: Definition-level sources and original finite calculations; independent review pending.

grammar.formation_rule: Use q for the one-book probability. The remaining probability is 1−q; r sends its selected share to two books and 1−r sends the rest to zero books. Thus p₀=(1−q)(1−r), p₁=q and p₂=(1−q)r. For a positive mass use I(xᵢ)=−log₂pᵢ bits. Multiply by pᵢ and add the contributions to obtain H(X). A zero-probability contribution is defined as zero by continuity.
grammar.precedence: Compute a logarithm only for a positive mass, then negate, multiply by that mass and sum. Use the zero-term convention separately at an impossible outcome.

properties.claim: Entropy is nonnegative and vanishes for a certain outcome.
properties.conditions: Use finite probabilities with base-two logarithms and the zero-term convention.
properties.derivation: For 0<p≤1, −log₂p≥0. A unit mass has −log₂1=0; every other term has zero mass.
properties.status: author-derived for stated conditions; independent mathematical review pending

properties.claim: Uniform masses maximize entropy on the three listed values.
properties.conditions: The full probability vector has three nonnegative entries adding to one.
properties.derivation: The finite entropy bound H≤log₂3 has equality at (1/3,1/3,1/3). The formal proof is in the source references; the display shows this family.

prompts.prompt: Why does an impossible outcome contribute zero?
prompts.answer: The function −p log₂p approaches zero as positive p approaches zero; the entropy sum uses that continuous extension.

prompts.prompt: Does entropy have the same units as the mean?
prompts.answer: No. The expected count has units of books. Base-two Shannon entropy has units of bits.
